title: Charge-Pump PLLs
intro: Adding frequency detection and a charge pump fixes the type I loop's narrow acquisition range and its static phase error, at the cost of a stability problem that a single resistor solves (Razavi, Section 16.2).

blocks.text: Lock acquisition

When the loop starts far from lock the PD sees two different frequencies and its output averages to nearly nothing. A type I loop acquires lock only if the frequency difference is roughly within $\omega_{LPF}$, which shrinks as the filter is made quieter. Since the VCO's free-running frequency can be far off over process and temperature, modern PLLs add frequency detection: a frequency-feedback path pulls the VCO near the input, then the phase loop takes over. This widens the acquisition range to the VCO's tuning range.
Phase/frequency detector

For periodic inputs one sequential circuit can do both jobs. Two flip-flops with their D inputs tied high are clocked by the reference A and the feedback B; an AND gate resets both when both outputs are high. A rising edge on A sets $Q_A$ (UP) until the next edge on B, and vice versa. If A leads, $Q_A$ pulses with width proportional to the phase difference; if A is faster, $Q_A$ pulses and $Q_B$ stays mostly low. So the sign of $\overline{Q_A} - \overline{Q_B}$ always says which way to steer, even when the frequencies differ.

The characteristic $\overline{Q_A} - \overline{Q_B}$ is linear over $\pm 2\pi$ (not $\pm\pi$ as for an XOR). Even at zero phase error both outputs go high together briefly before the reset propagates, roughly five gate delays (through the AND gate and the flip-flops' internal latches).

blocks.alt: Two D flip-flops with D tied to logic one, clocked by A and B. Their Q outputs, UP and DN, feed an AND gate whose output resets both flip-flops. UP closes switch S1 connecting current source I1 from VDD to the output node; DN closes S2 connecting the node to current source I2 to ground. The node drives a series resistor RP and capacitor CP to ground, a capacitor C2 to ground, and the VCO control input.
blocks.caption: PFD, charge pump and loop filter.

blocks.text: Charge pump

A charge pump is two switched current sources: UP connects $I_1$ into the filter, DN connects $I_2$ out of it, nominally equal $I_P$. Into a plain capacitor $C_P$, a constant phase error makes UP pulse every cycle, so $V_{cont}$ ramps forever: the PFD/CP/capacitor combination has infinite DC gain. That is the point: in lock $V_{cont}$ is finite, so the phase error must be exactly zero (apart from mismatches).

Its transfer function: a phase step $\phi_0$ gives pulses $\phi_0 T_{in}/2\pi$ wide each period, raising $V_{cont}$ by $(I_P/C_P)\phi_0T_{in}/2\pi$ per period. Treating the staircase as a ramp (valid when the loop is slow compared with the reference) and differentiating the step response:
The type II loop and its zero

With the VCO's $K_{VCO}/s$, the loop gain has two poles at the origin (type II): $\frac{I_P K_{VCO}}{2\pi C_P s^2}$. The closed loop then has poles on the $j\omega$ axis and oscillates: two ideal integrators give a flat −180°. A resistor $R_P$ in series with $C_P$ adds a zero:

blocks.alt: Top: loop-gain magnitude falling at 40 dB per decade at low frequency and 20 dB per decade above the zero; a dashed line continues at 40 dB per decade. Bottom: phase starting at minus 180 degrees and rising toward minus 90 degrees above the zero.
blocks.caption: Type II loop gain with the stabilizing zero.

blocks.text: Stability behaviour

Unlike the type I loop, more loop gain makes a type II loop more stable: lowering $I_PK_{VCO}$ moves the crossover toward the origin, where the phase is near −180°. On the root locus, both poles start at the origin and move on a circle centred at $-1/(R_PC_P)$ with radius $1/(R_PC_P)$, meeting the real axis at $-2/(R_PC_P)$ when $\zeta = 1$; then one heads to $-1/(R_PC_P)$ and the other to $-\infty$. (Reading −180° off the Bode plot at very low frequency and predicting oscillation is a mistake: the phase is slightly above −180° there, and Nyquist shows two integrators plus a zero do not oscillate.)

The continuous-time model breaks down when $R_P$ gets very large: the discrete nature of the charge pump makes the loop less stable again, so simulations set the real bounds. A common rule keeps the loop bandwidth around a tenth of the reference frequency or below.
Ripple and the second capacitor

Every pump pulse drives $I_P$ through $R_P$, so $V_{cont}$ jumps by $I_PR_P$ for the pulse duration; mismatch and switch charge injection cause such jumps even in lock. A capacitor $C_2$ across the $R_P$-$C_P$ branch smooths them. The loop becomes third order, but with $C_2$ about $C_P/5$ to $C_P/10$ the response barely changes.
With a divider

A divide-by-$M$ in the feedback path makes the VCO and divider look like one VCO with gain $K_{VCO}/M$, so replace $K_{VCO}$ by $K_{VCO}/M$ in $\omega_n$, $\zeta$ and $1/(\zeta\omega_n) = 4\pi M/(R_PI_PK_{VCO})$: division hurts both stability and settling unless $I_P$ is raised to match.

More depth: PLL Building Blocks covers PFD circuits and their dead and blind zones, charge-pump topologies and current matching, reference-spur estimates, and closed-form loop-filter design for a chosen phase margin.

blocks.title: Charge per cycle
blocks.text: A charge pump with $I_P = 100\ \mu\text{A}$ drives $C_P = 10\text{ pF}$ directly. The reference is 10 MHz and the feedback lags by 0.1 rad. How much does $V_{cont}$ rise per reference cycle?
solution: $\Delta V = (I_P/C_P)\times 1.59\text{ ns} = 10^7\text{ V/s} \times 1.59\text{ ns} = 15.9\text{ mV}$, every cycle, until the error is removed.

blocks.title: Designing a loop filter
blocks.text: A 2.5 GHz synthesizer uses a 25 MHz reference ($M = 100$), $K_{VCO} = 2\pi \times 1\text{ GHz/V}$, $I_P = 200\ \mu\text{A}$ and $C_P = 50\text{ pF}$. Find $\omega_n$, the $R_P$ for $\zeta = 1$, the zero frequency and a value for $C_2$.
solution: $\omega_n = \sqrt{I_PK_{VCO}/(2\pi C_PM)} = \sqrt{(2\times10^{-4})(6.28\times10^9)/(6.28 \cdot 5\times10^{-11}\cdot 100)} = \sqrt{4\times10^{13}} = 6.32\times10^6\text{ rad/s}$ (1.0 MHz, a 25th of the reference).
$\zeta = \frac{R_P}{2}\sqrt{I_PC_PK_{VCO}/(2\pi M)}$; the root is $\sqrt{10^{-7}} = 3.16\times10^{-4}$, so $R_P = 2/3.16\times10^{-4} = 6.3\text{ k}\Omega$.
Check: at $\zeta = 1$ both poles sit at $-2/(R_PC_P) = -6.32\times10^6$, equal to $-\omega_n$, and $1/(\zeta\omega_n) = 158\text{ ns}$.
blocks.answer: $\omega_n = 6.3\times10^6$ rad/s, $R_P \approx 6.3\text{ k}\Omega$, zero at $3.2\times10^6$ rad/s, $C_2 \approx 5\text{ pF}$.

blocks.title: Loop dynamics
blocks.text: $I_P = 100\ \mu\text{A}$, $K_{VCO} = 2\pi \times 500\text{ MHz/V} = 3.14\times10^9$ rad/s/V, $N = 100$, $C_1 = 10\text{ pF}$. Find $\omega_n$ and $f_n$.
solution: $f_n = 1.13\text{ MHz}$, about a tenth of a 10 MHz reference, at the edge of the usual limit.

blocks.title: Ripple step
blocks.text: In the previous design ($I_P = 200\ \mu\text{A}$, $R_P = 6.3\text{ k}\Omega$), how big is the jump on $V_{cont}$ during a pump pulse without $C_2$, and how much does it move the VCO?
solution: With $K_{VCO} = 1$ GHz/V the VCO would jump by over a gigahertz during each pulse. Hence $C_2$, which absorbs the pulse charge and turns the jump into a small step.
blocks.answer: About 1.3 V, which is why $C_2$ is needed.
